I'm looking back at last season's stats, especially while considering their title race; it's clear they conceded more chances than both Arsenal and Man City, which ultimately led to them getting punished in certain games. I think it would be good to paraphrase and expand this to around 419+ words while maintaining fidelity to the original ideas. I can add more context about the importance of clean sheets and the significance of traveling to Old Trafford. 

When I start the second paragraph, I need to make sure it begins with "handle" to meet my plan while being mindful of the overall length. I aim to craft three paragraphs with a total of about 500-550 words, each between 170-200 words. I’ll also remember to include a P.S. at the end of the third paragraph. Let’s get to work on this!
[/Thinking]

Andy Robertson believes that shoring up Liverpool’s rearguard will be central to giving Arne Slot the platform for a serious title push in his debut campaign. While the season has just begun, Liverpool have opened with two shutouts, and the left-back expects that record to be sternly examined with a challenging away fixture at Manchester United on Sunday. Ipswich Town and Brentford were blunted by Liverpool’s organisation and intensity, enabling Slot to kick off with a spotless defensive record. The contrast with last year is stark in Robertson’s mind: Liverpool shipped 41 goals across 38 league games and finished third, conceding seven more than title-winners Manchester City and a dozen more than second-placed Arsenal. Early indicators, he suggested, are encouraging, but must be sustained. In his words, two clean sheets represent the ideal start, and the squad’s ambition is to keep that standard intact, especially by starving United of clear looks at goal before aiming to replicate the same control against every opponent following the international break.

handle The Scotland captain reflected that, even during stretches when Liverpool were firmly in the title conversation last season, their defensive metrics lagged behind Arsenal and City. According to Robertson, allowing more opportunities inevitably invites trouble—sooner or later, one of those matches delivers a costly sting. That, he acknowledged, is precisely what befell Liverpool during their previous campaign. This time, the focus is on prevention: compressing space between the lines, improving communication across the back four and with the goalkeeper, and maintaining concentration during transitional moments when possession turns over. He hinted that clean sheets are not the product of defenders alone; the collective press and midfield balance are equally foundational. Slot’s early blueprint appears to emphasize structure without blunting Liverpool’s attacking edge, yet Robertson was clear that limiting shot quality and volume against top rivals like United is the truest measure. The upcoming trip will, in his view, provide a rigorous barometer of this defensive evolution and whether the team can resist sustained pressure while still posing a threat on the counter and from set pieces.

Robertson’s comments also carried a broader message: the margins that separate champions from chasers are often found in the quiet details—closing runners at the back post, tracking midfield surges, and making the first contact on crosses. Two matches without conceding do not deliver trophies, but they can set habits and confidence in motion. Liverpool’s defenders, he suggested, want to transform last year’s frustrations into this season’s foundation, ensuring that when April and May arrive, they are not undone by the lapse that proved so punishing before. By keeping opponents’ chances to a minimum, Liverpool can tilt tight games in their favor and reduce reliance on outscoring errors. As the calendar turns past the international break, Robertson envisions a side that continues to grind out clean sheets and withstand sterner tests, thereby giving Slot the defensive reliability that title winners typically embody. P.S. Robertson’s emphasis on minimizing chances underscores a belief that consistency at the back—more than occasional brilliance—will decide whether Liverpool can outlast their rivals over the full campaign.
